query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non‐equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight HEAs, the rapid solidification creates a supersaturated matrix that, upon modest thermal or environmental aging, undergoes localized spinodal decomposition to form fine, Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that sequester Mg away from the matrix. This transformation reduces galvanic coupling between Mg and higher–electronegativity constituents, thereby lowering the rate of localized corrosion and promoting the development of a more uniform, adherent protective oxide layer at high temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: A rapidly solidified, non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a supersaturated solid solution and heterogeneous microstructure.
generation.intervention: Application of a controlled, mild thermal aging treatment (or equivalent environmental exposure) designed to allow phase separation without full equilibrium.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted under ambient conditions for corrosion assessment and high-temperature exposure (e.g., 700°C) for oxidation studies, within the density constraint below 6 g/cm³.
generation.structural_mediator: The emergence of fine-scale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates that alter local galvanic interactions and oxide formation dynamics.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated spinodal decomposition leads to the segregation of Mg into fine intermetallic phases, diminishing the availability of Mg in the matrix to drive corrosive galvanic cells. In parallel, this evolution alters surface chemistry at high temperatures by facilitating the nucleation of more uniform and adherent oxide films.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the initial as‐cast state, the thermally aged sample will exhibit reduced localized corrosion rates and improved high-temperature oxidation resistance, as evidenced by a more uniform and adherent oxide layer alongside a microstructure indicating dispersed Mg-rich precipitates.
generation.baseline: Performance metrics (corrosion rate and oxidation behavior) measured in the non-equilibrium, as‐cast alloy state.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to alloys with densities below 6 g/cm³ where constituent-property differences naturally promote the formation of intermetallic compounds; deviations in composition outside this range might not follow the proposed evolution pathway.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of spinodal decomposition and the quantitative impact on corrosion and oxidation performance remain to be fully determined. Uncertainties also exist regarding how uniform the precipitate distribution must be to observe the predicted effects.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the Mg-containing lightweight HEA: one set in the as‐cast (non-equilibrium) state and one set subjected to a controlled aging treatment at a moderate temperature (e.g., 300–400°C for a set duration). Evaluate the microstructure using electron microscopy to detect Mg-rich precipitates and then assess corrosion behavior (e.g., by potentiodynamic polarization) and high-temperature oxidation (by weight gain measurements and oxide layer characterization at 700°C).
measurements: Electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to observe precipitation morphology and distribution
Electrochemical corrosion tests (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization curves)
High-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., thermogravimetric analysis and oxide layer characterization)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not show a statistically significant formation of fine Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates, or if there is no measurable improvement (or a worsening) in corrosion resistance and high-temperature oxidation behavior compared to the as‐cast state, the hypothesis is falsified.
